papers.title_in_file: Quantum supremacy using a programmable superconducting processor
papers.what_it_is: Google AI Quantum's Nature article reporting random circuit sampling on the 53-qubit Sycamore superconducting processor, with cross-entropy benchmarking and a classical cost estimate used to claim quantum supremacy.

existing.certainty_reason: The paper states the circuit size and the model prediction in the section on building the processor.

existing.note: The stored value is right. The paper adds that the expected lower simulation costs will be consistently outpaced by hardware improvements, and it names the three variations (patch, elided, verification circuits). The stored anchor 'Methods and Discussion' is not a section of this text; the sentences are in 'Fidelity estimation in the supremacy regime' and 'The classical computational cost'.
existing.value: The authors state that they cannot compute FXEB in the supremacy regime and estimate it with three simplified circuit variants (patch, elided and verification circuits). They also state that they expect lower classical simulation costs than reported to eventually be achieved, but expect those costs to be consistently outpaced by hardware improvements on larger quantum processors.
existing.anchor: Section 'Fidelity estimation in the supremacy regime', p.508; Section 'The classical computational cost', p.509
quotes: Although we cannot compute FXEB in the supremacy regime, we can estimate it using three variations to reduce the complexity of the circuits.
We expect that lower simulation costs than reported here will eventually be achieved, but we also expect that they will be consistently outpaced by hardware improvements on larger quantum processors.
existing.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limit (FXEB cannot be computed in the supremacy regime) in the section on fidelity estimation.
existing.reader_inference: The second sentence is an expectation of the authors, not a result; it is a forecast, and the paper gives no evidence for it.

existing.note: The 10,000 years is an estimate by extrapolation, not a measured run. The Figure 4 caption limits it to circuits with 20 cycles, to equal-fidelity classical sampling (0.1% fidelity in the text), and to a million cores. The abstract says the benchmarks 'currently indicate' it.
existing.value: The authors report that Sycamore takes about 200 seconds to sample one instance of a quantum circuit a million times, and that their benchmarks currently indicate the equivalent task for a state-of-the-art classical supercomputer would take approximately 10,000 years. The caption of the benchmarking figure states the setting: for 20 cycles, obtaining a million samples on the quantum processor takes 200 seconds, whereas an equal-fidelity classical sampling would take 10,000 years on a million cores.
quotes: Our Sycamore processor takes about 200 seconds to sample one instance of a quantum circuit a million times
our benchmarks currently indicate that the equivalent task for a state-of-the-art classical supercomputer would take approximately 10,000 years
For m = 20, obtaining a million samples on the quantum processor takes 200 seconds, whereas an equal-fidelity classical sampling would take 10,000 years on a million cores
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; the classical figure is an extrapolated estimate.
existing.reader_inference: The 200 seconds is a measured quantum run time; the 10,000 years is an extrapolation from partial classical runs (see the cost section), so the two numbers are not the same kind of evidence.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Sycamore processor is a two-dimensional array of 54 transmon qubits, each tunably coupled to four nearest neighbours, and that one qubit did not function properly, so the device uses 53 qubits and 86 couplers.
quotes: consists of a two-dimensional array of 54 transmon qubits, where each qubit is tunably coupled to four nearest neighbours, in a rectangular lattice
One qubit did not function properly, so the device uses 53 qubits and 86 couplers.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own description of its device, in the section on building the processor.

assertions.value: The authors state that the chip is cooled to below 20 mK in a dilution refrigerator, that 277 digital-to-analog converters are used for complete control, and that the adjustable coupler tunes the qubit-qubit coupling from completely off to 40 MHz.
quotes: cooled to below 20 mK in a dilution refrigerator
we orchestrate 277 digital-to-analog converters (14 bits at 1 GHz)
tune the qubit–qubit coupling from completely off to 40 MHz
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own description of the apparatus.

assertions.value: The authors state that single-qubit gates are 25-ns microwave pulses, and that the two-qubit iSWAP-like gate turns on a 20-MHz coupling for 12 ns.
quotes: We execute single-qubit gates by driving 25-ns microwave pulses resonant with the qubit frequency
turning on a 20-MHz coupling for 12 ns
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own description of its gate settings.

assertions.value: The authors define the linear cross-entropy benchmarking fidelity as 2 to the power n times the mean, over the observed bitstrings, of the ideal probability of each bitstring, minus 1, where n is the number of qubits. The text layer printed the exponent flat.
assertions.anchor: Section 'A suitable computational task', Equation (1), p.506
quotes: FXEB = 2n⟨P(xi)⟩i − 1
where n is the number of qubits, P(xi) is the probability of bitstring xi computed for the ideal quantum circuit, and the average is over the observed bitstrings
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines FXEB in Equation (1) and the results depend on it.

assertions.value: The authors state that without errors the probability distribution is exponential and sampling from it produces FXEB equal to 1, that sampling from the uniform distribution produces FXEB equal to 0, and that the probabilities must be obtained by classically simulating the circuit, so computing FXEB is intractable in the regime of quantum supremacy.
quotes: sampling from this distribution will produce FXEB = 1.
sampling from the uniform distribution will give ⟨P(xi)⟩i = 1/2n and produce FXEB = 0.
thus computing FXEB is intractable in the regime of quantum supremacy
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the limits of its own benchmark in the section that introduces it.

assertions.value: The authors report an average two-qubit Pauli error e2 of 0.36% when two-qubit circuits run in isolation and 0.62% when two-qubit circuits run simultaneously over the entire array. Figure 2 lists the average errors, in the order single-qubit e1, two-qubit e2, two-qubit per cycle e2c and readout er, as 0.15%, 0.36%, 0.65% and 3.1% in isolation, and 0.16%, 0.62%, 0.93% and 3.8% when simultaneous.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Building a high-fidelity processor', p.507; Fig. 2 table, p.507
quotes: We find an average e2 of 0.36%.
we find an average e2 of 0.62%.
Single-qubit (e1) Two-qubit (e2) Two-qubit, cycle (e2c) Readout (er) b Pauli error e1, e2
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The column order of the Figure 2 table is read from the order of the labels in the text layer; the figure itself was not seen.

assertions.value: The authors state that running all qubits executing single-qubit gates simultaneously shows only a small increase in the error probabilities, which they say demonstrates low microwave crosstalk, and that simultaneous readout incurs only a modest increase in per-qubit measurement errors.
quotes: which shows only a small increase in the error probabilities, demonstrating that our device has low microwave crosstalk
simultaneous readout incurs only a modest increase in per-qubit measurement errors
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the full experiment uses the two-qubit unitaries measured for each pair during simultaneous operation rather than a standard gate, that the typical two-qubit gate is a full iSWAP with 1/6th of a full CZ, and that implementing high-fidelity textbook gates natively is work in progress.
quotes: we generate quantum circuits using the twoqubit unitaries measured for each pair during simultaneous operation, rather than a standard gate for all pairs
The typical two-qubit gate is a full iSWAP with 1/6th of a full CZ.
is work in progress.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the gate set it used and that native textbook gates are not yet implemented.

assertions.value: The authors state that they model the fidelity of a quantum circuit as the product of the probabilities of error-free operation of all gates and measurements, and that this model assumes entangling larger systems does not introduce additional error sources beyond those measured at the single- and two-qubit level.
quotes: we can model the fidelity of a quantum circuit as the product of the probabilities of error-free operation of all gates and measurements
Our model assumes that entangling larger and larger systems does not introduce additional error sources beyond the errors we measure at the single- and two-qubit level.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own model and the assumption behind it.

assertions.value: The authors describe three circuit variants used to estimate fidelity: patch circuits remove a slice of two-qubit gates so the circuit splits into two non-interacting patches; elided circuits remove only a fraction of the initial two-qubit gates along the slice, which allows entanglement between patches; verification circuits have the same gate counts as the supremacy circuits but a different two-qubit gate sequence that is much easier to simulate classically.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Fidelity estimation in the supremacy regime', p.508
quotes: we remove a slice of two-qubit gates (a small fraction of the total number of two-qubit gates), splitting the circuit into two spatially isolated, non-interacting patches of qubits
we remove only a fraction of the initial two-qubit gates along the slice, allowing for entanglement between patches
with the same gate counts as our supremacy circuits, but with a different pattern for the sequence of two-qubit gates, which is much easier to simulate classically
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the three variants its fidelity estimates depend on.

assertions.value: The authors report that the patch and elided versions of the verification circuits produce the same fidelity as the full verification circuits up to 53 qubits, and that the predicted, patch and elided fidelities all show good agreement with the fidelities of the corresponding full circuits. For each data point they typically collect a total of five million samples over ten circuit instances.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Fidelity estimation in the supremacy regime', Fig. 4a, p.508
quotes: We first check that the patch and elided versions of the verification circuits produce the same fidelity as the full verification circuits up to 53 qubits
The predicted, patch and elided fidelities all show good agreement with the fidelities of the corresponding full circuits
we typically collect Ns = 5 × 106 total samples over ten circuit instances
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The agreement is shown for the simplifiable gate sequence; the paper extends it to the hard sequence by inference (see the elided-circuit assertion).

assertions.value: The authors report that the largest circuits whose fidelity can still be directly verified have 53 qubits and a simplified gate arrangement, and that performing random circuit sampling on these at 0.8% fidelity takes one million cores 130 seconds, which they describe as a million-fold speedup of the quantum processor relative to a single core.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Fidelity estimation in the supremacy regime', p.508
quotes: The largest circuits for which the fidelity can still be directly verified have 53 qubits and a simplified gate arrangement.
Performing random circuit sampling on these at 0.8% fidelity takes one million cores 130 seconds, corresponding to a million-fold speedup of the quantum processor relative to a single core.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: This is the simplified gate arrangement, not the supremacy circuits; the 10,000-year figure does not apply to it.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the largest circuit, with 53 qubits and 20 cycles, they collected 30 million samples over ten circuit instances and obtained an FXEB of 2.24 plus or minus 0.21, times ten to the power minus three, for the elided circuits. The text layer printed the exponent flat.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Fidelity estimation in the supremacy regime', Fig. 4b, p.508
quotes: For the largest circuit with 53 qubits and 20 cycles, we collected Ns = 30 × 106 samples over ten circuit instances
obtaining FXEB = (2.24 ±0.21) × 10−3 for the elided circuits
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The measured value is on elided circuits, which are simulable; the full supremacy circuits were not simulated.

assertions.value: The authors state that, with 5 sigma confidence, the average fidelity of running these circuits on the quantum processor is greater than at least 0.1%, and the caption of the benchmarking figure states that sigma includes both systematic and statistical uncertainties.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Fidelity estimation in the supremacy regime', p.508; Fig. 4 caption, p.509
quotes: With 5σ confidence, we assert that the average fidelity
of running these circuits on the quantum processor is greater than at least 0.1%
where σ includes both systematic and statistical uncertainties
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that they expect the full data for the supremacy-regime figure to have similar fidelities, but that the simulation times take too long to check, so the data were archived rather than verified.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Fidelity estimation in the supremacy regime', p.508; Fig. 4 caption, p.509
quotes: We expect that the full data for Fig. 4b should have similar fidelities
since the simulation times (red numbers) take too long to check, we have archived the data
The corresponding full circuit data, not simulated but archived, is expected to show similarly statistically significant fidelity.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states that the full supremacy-regime fidelity was not checked.
assertions.reader_inference: The supremacy-regime fidelity of the full circuits is inferred from elided circuits, not measured against simulation.

assertions.value: The authors state that up to 43 qubits they use a Schrödinger algorithm, with the Jülich supercomputer (100,000 cores, 250 terabytes) running the largest cases, and that above this size there is not enough random access memory to store the quantum state, so they use a hybrid Schrödinger-Feynman algorithm on Google data centres.
quotes: Up to 43 qubits, we use a Schrödinger algorithm, which simulates the evolution of the full quantum state
the Jülich supercomputer (with 100,000 cores, 250 terabytes) runs the largest cases
we use a hybrid Schrödinger–Feynman algorithm43 running on Google data centres to compute the amplitudes of individual bitstrings
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own description of the classical simulations it ran.

assertions.value: The authors state that they estimated the classical cost of the supremacy circuits by running portions of the simulation on the Summit supercomputer and on Google clusters and extrapolating to the full cost, and that they account for the cost of sampling by scaling the verification cost with FXEB, for example a 0.1% fidelity decreases the cost by about 1,000.
quotes: we ran portions of the quantum circuit simulation on both the Summit supercomputer as well as on Google clusters and extrapolated to the full cost
we account for the computation cost of sampling by scaling the verification cost with FXEB
a 0.1% fidelity decreases the cost by about 1,000
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical estimate from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The classical figures in the paper rest on extrapolation and on a cost model that scales with FXEB.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the Summit supercomputer the tensors do not reasonably fit into node memory at 20 cycles, so they measured runtimes only up to 14 cycles, for which they estimate that sampling three million bitstrings with 1% fidelity would require a year.
quotes: At m = 20 the tensors do not reasonably fit into node memory, so we can only measure runtimes up to m = 14
for which we estimate that sampling three million bitstrings with 1% fidelity would require a year
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical estimate from one study.

assertions.value: The authors estimate that on Google Cloud servers, performing the same task for 20 cycles with 0.1% fidelity using the Schrödinger-Feynman algorithm would cost 50 trillion core-hours and consume one petawatt hour of energy.
quotes: we estimate that performing the same task for m = 20 with 0.1% fidelity using the Schrödinger–Feynman algorithm would cost 50 trillion core-hours and consume one petawatt hour of energy
assertions.certainty_reason: An estimate from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that it took 600 seconds to sample the circuit on the quantum processor three million times, that sampling time is limited by control hardware communications, and that the net quantum processor time is only about 30 seconds.
quotes: it took 600 seconds to sample the circuit on the quantum processor three million times
where sampling time is limited by control hardware communications
quantum processor time is only about 30 seconds
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract's 200 seconds is for one million samples; the 600 seconds here is for three million samples.

assertions.value: The authors state in a figure caption that verifying the fidelity of the supremacy circuits would take millions of years.
quotes: and verifying the fidelity would take millions of years
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's estimate without a derivation in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that their assumption, based on insights from complexity theory, is that the cost of this algorithmic task is exponential in circuit size, and that simulation methods have improved steadily over the past few years.
quotes: Our assumption, based on insights from complexity theory11–13, is that the cost of this algorithmic task is exponential in circuit size.
Indeed, simulation methods have improved steadily over the past few years
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own assumption behind the classical cost estimate.
assertions.reader_inference: Hardness of the task is assumed, not proved, in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that their experimental observations support the validity of the digital error model for their processor, because system fidelity is well predicted by a simple model in which the individually characterized fidelities of each gate are multiplied together.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Verifying the digital error model', p.509
quotes: our experimental observations support the validity of this model for our processor
Our system fidelity is well predicted by a simple model in which the individually characterized fidelities of each gate are multiplied together (Fig. 4).
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that they achieve low correlated errors by choosing circuits that randomize and decorrelate errors, by optimizing control to minimize systematic errors and leakage, and by designing gates that operate much faster than correlated noise sources such as 1/f flux noise.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Verifying the digital error model', p.509
quotes: choosing circuits that randomize and decorrelate errors, by optimizing control to minimize systematic errors and leakage
designing gates that operate much faster than correlated noise sources, such as 1/f flux noise
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states how its own experiment was designed.

assertions.value: The authors state that a single bit or phase flip over the course of the algorithm will completely shuffle the speckle pattern and result in close to zero fidelity, so a quantum processor with sufficiently low error rates is needed to claim quantum supremacy.
quotes: A single bit or phase flip over the course of the algorithm will completely shuffle the speckle pattern and result in close to zero fidelity
in order to claim quantum supremacy we need a quantum processor that executes the program with sufficiently low error rates
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim, cited to earlier work, not proved in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that random circuits are a suitable benchmark because they do not possess structure and therefore allow for limited guarantees of computational hardness.
quotes: Random circuits are a suitable choice for benchmarking because they do not possess structure and therefore allow for limited guarantees of computational hardness
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the limited scope of the hardness guarantees for its own task.
assertions.reader_inference: The guarantees are described as limited, so the hardness of the task is not established as a theorem here.

assertions.value: The authors claim that, to their knowledge, this experiment marks the first computation that can be performed only on a quantum processor, and that quantum processors have thus reached the regime of quantum supremacy.
quotes: To our knowledge, this experiment marks the first computation that can be performed only on a quantum processor.
Quantum processors have thus reached the regime of quantum supremacy.
assertions.certainty_reason: The company's authors describing their own result.
assertions.reader_inference: The claim rests on the classical cost estimate, which the paper itself says may fall.

assertions.value: The authors state that they expect the computational power of quantum processors to continue to grow at a double-exponential rate, and that sustaining this and running well known algorithms such as Shor or Grover will need the engineering of quantum error correction to become a focus of attention.
quotes: We expect that their computational power will continue to grow at a double-exponential rate
the engineering of quantum error correction will need to become a focus of attention.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's forecast without evidence in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that realizing the full promise of quantum computing, for example Shor's algorithm for factoring, still requires technical leaps to engineer fault-tolerant logical qubits.
quotes: still requires technical leaps to engineer fault-tolerant logical qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states a limit of what its experiment shows.

assertions.value: The authors state that their experiment suggests a model of computation may now be available that violates the extended Church-Turing thesis, and that they performed random quantum circuit sampling in polynomial time on a physically realizable quantum processor while no efficient method is known to exist for classical computing machinery.
quotes: Our experiment suggests that a model of computation may now be available that violates this
We have performed random quantum circuit sampling in polynomial time using a physically realizable quantum processor
yet no efficient method is known to exist for classical computing machinery
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim; the statement is hedged ('suggests') and rests on the classical cost assumption.

assertions.value: The authors state that the benchmark task has an immediate application in generating certifiable random numbers, citing a manuscript in preparation by S. Aaronson.
quotes: has an immediate application in generating certifiable random numbers (S. Aaronson, manuscript in preparation)
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result from work not yet available when the paper was published.
